title: Carbon system variables against the GLODAPv2 mapped climatology
model_year: 2002, day-weighted annual mean of the twelve months
reference: GLODAPv2.2016b mapped climatology, input data spanning 1972-2013, no time axis

method.units: dissic and talk converted from mol m-3 to umol/kg with an in-situ density field computed from each model's own thetao and so at each cell's own pressure; pH is dimensionless and untouched

density_note.CESM2: density field, read as an anomaly (sigma, + 1000) from its long_name, 'In-situ density anomaly'; 1005.1 to 1031.5 kg/m3 cell by cell (each cell's own in-situ pressure); converted at each cell's own density
density_note.GFDL-ESM4: density field, read as an anomaly (sigma, + 1000) from its long_name, 'In-situ density anomaly'; 996.3 to 1045.3 kg/m3 cell by cell (each cell's own in-situ pressure); converted at each cell's own density
density_note.MPI-ESM1-2-LR: density field, read as an anomaly (sigma, + 1000) from its long_name, 'In-situ density anomaly'; 1003.5 to 1035.8 kg/m3 cell by cell (each cell's own in-situ pressure); converted at each cell's own density

method.ph_field: GLODAP pHtsinsitutp (total scale, in-situ T and P), which is the quantity CMIP6 ph reports; pHts25p0 is a different quantity
method.step1_vs_step4: step 1 takes a volume-weighted mean on each source's own levels; step 4 interpolates onto common levels. A volume-weighted mean is not conserved by interpolation, and a bias at a named depth cannot be read off levels that differ between products
method.grid: every global mean on the model's native grid with its own volcello; regridding only for steps 3 and 4 and the display maps

findings: The model fields had to be converted with an in-situ density field rather than a constant. DIC and alkalinity are absolute concentrations, so unlike a ratio or a depth the conversion moves every number, and a constant near-surface density would err by about the size of the biases reported here.
On surface DIC the smallest bias against GLODAP is GFDL-ESM4 (+23 micromoles per kilogram).

Step 5 is what decides how much of the DIC bias can be read as model error. The period change each model shows between its 1971-2000 mean and 2002 is CESM2 +9, GFDL-ESM4 +12, MPI-ESM1-2-LR +11 micromoles per kilogram, against biases of CESM2 -39, GFDL-ESM4 +23, MPI-ESM1-2-LR -61. Where those are comparable in size the bias is sensitive to the year sampled.

That period change is mostly the forced rise of surface DIC as the ocean takes up anthropogenic CO2 between the two periods, plus internal variability. It is not model drift in the CMIP6 sense - the residual trend of the pre-industrial control run - which cannot be measured here without a piControl run.
Alkalinity is far less sensitive to anthropogenic CO2 than DIC, so its bias cannot be explained by the period mismatch and is the cleaner indicator of a structural model error.

The DIC and alkalinity biases carry the SAME SIGN in every model - CESM2 -39 and -40, GFDL-ESM4 +23 and +31, MPI-ESM1-2-LR -61 and -87 micromoles per kilogram - which is why pH comes out far better than either variable alone. pH responds to the balance between the two, so errors that move DIC and alkalinity together largely cancel in it: CESM2 is off by -39 in DIC and -40 in alkalinity yet reproduces pH to 0.001. Agreement in pH alone is therefore NOT evidence that a model's carbon system is right, and the three variables have to be read together - which is what this case is built to show.
